title: Technology Adoption and Productivity Growth: Evidence from Industrialization in France
abstract: New technologies tend to be adopted slowly and—even after being adopted—take time to be reflected in higher aggregate productivity. One prominent explanation is that major technological breakthroughs create the need to reorganize production. We study a unique setting that allows us to examine this mechanism: the adoption of mechanized cotton spinning during the first Industrial Revolution in France. Using a novel hand-collected, plant-level dataset from French archival sources, we show that a process of “trial and error” in reorganizing production led to initially low and widely dispersed productivity across firms operating the new technology. In the subsequent decades, we observe high productivity growth as knowledge diffused through the economy and new entrants adopted improved methods of organizing production.
summary_en: Why does productivity often fail to rise immediately when firms adopt a new technology? Juhász, Squicciarini and Voigtländer argue the answer is reorganisation cost: firms must rearrange production around the new technology, and they learn by trial and error. Using hand-collected plant-level data from French archives covering the early-19th-century mechanisation of cotton spinning, they document low and widely dispersed productivity in the first generation of mechanised plants. Productivity rose sharply over subsequent decades as knowledge of how to organise mechanised production diffused and new entrants adopted improved methods.
data_used: Hand-collected plant-level dataset from French archival records (departmental statistical surveys, prefectoral reports) on cotton-spinning mills 1800-1860, including output, employment, and capital measures for ~5,000 plants across France.
policy_relevance: Hungary's productivity gap with Western Europe persists despite high foreign-direct-investment and capital-intensive technology adoption. This paper provides theoretical grounding for why catch-up takes decades — reorganisation knowledge diffuses slowly. Useful for the Pénzügyminisztérium and HIPA when calibrating expectations for productivity payoffs from greenfield-investment subsidies.
